Action Plan:
1. Prescribe spacer device and peak-flow meter; pharmacist to demonstrate correct use.  
2. Increase salbutamol inhaler to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours via spacer until symptoms settle.  
3. Patient to record peak-flow readings morning and evening for the next 7 days.  
4. Arrange follow-up asthma review (telephone or face-to-face) in 1 week to discuss peak-flow diary and consider stepping-up asthma therapy if needed.  
5. Advise daily, regular, over-the-counter antihistamine for hay-fever control; pharmacist to recommend suitable product.  
6. Safety-net: if fever develops (>38 °C) or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens (especially at rest or with speech), patient to contact GP or emergency services immediately.  
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: 2–3 day history of wheeze and exertional shortness of breath.  
• Associated symptoms: dry cough, self-checked temperature 37 °C, occasional difficulty completing sentences; denies chest pain, nocturnal symptoms, hemoptysis.  
• Symptom impact: Unable to walk to work; currently works from home/takes sick leave.  
• Past medical history: Childhood and adult asthma (occasional hospital visits, never ICU), hay fever, eczema.  
• Medications: Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented; typically every few weeks and before exercise).  
• Allergies: No known drug allergies.  
• Social: Non-smoker; alcohol ~1 glass wine every 2–3 days; lives with partner; occupation—engineer.

Objective:
• Tele-consultation; no physical examination performed.  
• Patient-reported temperature: 37 °C.  
• No other vitals or examination findings available.  
• No investigations performed to date.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute asthma exacerbation  
   - Assessment: Likely mild–moderate flare of known asthma, possibly triggered by pollen exposure or viral URTI.  
   - Investigations planned: Prescribe peak-flow meter; patient to document readings twice daily.  
   - Treatment: Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours via newly prescribed spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate technique.  
   - Follow-up: Review in 1 week with peak-flow diary; escalate therapy if control remains poor.

2. Allergic rhinitis (hay fever)  
   - Assessment: Persistent seasonal allergy contributing to asthma flare.  
   - Treatment: Initiate regular oral antihistamine (specific product/dose not documented; OTC).  
   - Follow-up: Monitor symptom control at next review; consider further allergy management if required.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected elements: No current objective respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, or full medication list reconciliation.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional patient difficulty hearing questions but overall intelligible.
